endorsements.quote: For implementation within the proposed framework, Article 72 post-market monitoring is organised across three areas: technical, clinical, and organisational monitoring.
Clinical monitoring includes false positive and false negative rates, late diagnosis, adverse effects, subgroup analysis, and the physician’s practice of overriding the algorithm.
Organisational monitoring includes adherence to instructions for use, off-label use, staff training, and the implementation process.
This gap must be addressed at procurement through explicit contractual terms requiring Annex XII documentation as a condition of supply.
Monitoring responsibilities should be explicitly allocated between providers and deployers through procurement and governance arrangements ( 4 ).
Classification should precede final system development because it determines the applicable legal framework, validation requirements, instructions for use, and post-market obligations.

A material change in applicable legislation, regulatory guidance, or harmonised standards should also trigger reassessment of the Stage 2 regulatory governance map and, where relevant, revision of affected downstream artefacts.

Where datasets are obtained through the EHDS secondary-use framework, the applicable data permit, the responsible Health Data Access Body, the secure processing environment, the anonymisation or pseudonymisation status, and the permitted-purpose scope should all be documented ( 4 , 7 , 8 ).

Output: An overview of the human-oversight protocol, including user roles, training, escalation criteria, override procedures, documentation and accountability procedures, as well as Article 22 assessment.

Within the proposed framework, Article 14 human-oversight requirements are implemented through appropriate interfaces, user training, escalation policies, override controls, and accountability processes tailored to the relevant use case ( 4 ).

Configuration A requires clinician review before AI-generated content enters the medical record; Configuration B requires escalation procedures, uncertainty handling, and disclosure to patients that they are interacting with an AI system.

Output: A change-control and corrective-action file documenting the reason for each modification, affected system components, validation evidence, updated risk assessments, user communications, regulatory implications, deployment dates, rollback procedures, and post-update evaluation results.

The allocation of monitoring and change-control responsibility between the GPAI provider, the downstream high-risk provider, and the deployer therefore becomes a substantive governance question taken up at Stages 7 and 8 (Sections 8.7 – 8.8 ).

unlisted_practices: Classify AI systems by intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable use rather than solely by the manufacturer's marketing description or labelling.
Assess the interaction of the AI Act, MDR, IVDR, GDPR and EHDS and record it in a regulatory governance map with responsible actors.
Record the specific GDPR Article 9(2) condition and national legal basis relied upon for each data source used in AI development.
Justify and document bias-mitigation activities that rely on sensitive attributes against the strict-necessity threshold.
Assess dataset representativeness, subgroup disparities, and annotation quality before development and deployment, and assess data quality per the ISO/IEC 5259 series.
Report AI performance evaluation using recognised frameworks such as FUTURE-AI, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI and QUEST, aligned to the intended purpose rather than generic benchmarks.
Assess Article 22 GDPR implications of solely automated decisions alongside AI Act human oversight, and address clinicians routinely deferring to AI.

Integrate AI Act quality management and conformity assessment into existing MDR/IVDR processes and standards such as ISO 13485, ISO 14971, IEC 62304 and ISO/IEC 42001, maintaining an integrated assurance file.
Differentiate routine maintenance, retraining, intended-use change and substantial modification to determine when revalidation, user notification or renewed conformity assessment is required.
Treat retraining that alters clinically relevant performance characteristics as a substantial modification requiring renewed conformity assessment.
Suspend, restrict, or correct AI systems when residual risk is unacceptable, and investigate and report serious occurrences to regulators.

screen.reason: The paper provides a conceptual regulatory analysis and proposes a compliance-by-design framework/recommendations for governing medical AI under EU regulations, without empirical validation.
